entities.name: The Korean Classical Corpus
entities.label: Text
entities.summary: The Korean Classical Corpus encompasses the foundational historical, religious, literary, and linguistic texts of Korean civilization from the Three Kingdoms period through the Joseon dynasty. Key pillars include: the Samguk Sagi (1145 CE) — the oldest surviving Korean history, by Kim Busik, covering the Three Kingdoms of Silla, Goguryeo, and Baekje; the Samguk Yusa (1281 CE) — a compendium of Korean mythology, legend, and Buddhist history by the monk Iryeon, preserving the Dangun foundation myth; the Tripitaka Koreana (1237–1248 CE) — over 81,000 woodblocks of the entire Buddhist canon carved during the Mongol invasions as a prayer for national protection, representing the most complete and accurate version of the Chinese Buddhist canon and a UNESCO Memory of the World; and the Hunminjeongeum (1446 CE) — King Sejong the Great's promulgation of the Korean alphabetical script (Hangul), one of the most scientifically designed writing systems in human history, created so that "a wise man can acquaint himself with [the letters] before the morning is over; a stupid man can learn them in the space of ten days." This corpus reflects a civilization that, while deeply engaged with Chinese classical tradition, developed distinctive cultural, religious, and linguistic achievements.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Korean Classical Corpus preserves the foundational texts of Korean civilization, including the Samguk Sagi and Tripitaka Koreana, which provide critical insights into Korea's history, culture, and religious traditions. These texts have had a significant regional impact on East Asian cultural heritage.
